t: Sort the Features by Popularity with Count-Once Hashing
o: A feature is popular if users mention it, but each response votes for a feature at most once even if the word repeats inside it. So the task reduces to: count, per feature, how many response strings contain it as a whole word; then order features by that count descending, keeping original order on ties. In example 1, "touch" appears in two responses while "cooler" and "lock" appear in one each ("locker" does not count for "lock"), so the answer starts with touch and cooler precedes lock because it came first. Example 2 confirms repeated mentions like "a a a a a" still count once. Constraints are small (at most 10^4 features, 10^2 responses of up to 10^3 characters), so hashing plus one comparison sort is comfortably fast.
k: Count each response at most once per feature: dedupe the words of a response with a set before incrementing counters.
Ties keep original order: sort indices with an explicit index tie-break (or use a stable sort) instead of sorting name strings.
Popularity needs whole-word containment - "locker" must not boost "lock".

a.n: Approach 1: Per-Feature Scan Over Tokenized Responses
a.i: The most literal reading of the definition: split every response into a set of words once, then for each feature count how many of those word-sets contain it. Finally sort by descending count with ascending original index as tie-break. No cleverness, just two nested loops over features and responses.
s: Tokenize each response into a set of words.
For every feature, count the number of word-sets containing it.
Sort feature indices by descending count, then ascending index.
Return the features in that order.
a.t: O(F*T + F log F) - each of the F features is probed against all T total words across responses, plus the index sort
a.sp: O(T) - the token sets store every word of every response

a.i: Invert the loops: walk the responses once and add 1 to every distinct word each response contains. A hash map accumulates all popularities in a single sweep; features never mentioned simply stay absent (count 0). One final sort of indices with comparator (popularity desc, index asc) produces the answer.
s: For each response, iterate its distinct words (dedupe via a set) and increment each count.
Map sorted indices back to feature names.
a.t: O(T + F log F) - one counting sweep over all T words plus sorting F indices
a.sp: O(U) - the map holds only the U distinct words that actually occur

w: Use approach 2 in an interview; mention approach 1 only to motivate flipping the loop. Pitfalls: forgetting to dedupe words inside a response ("cooler cooler" counts once), breaking ties in the wrong direction (must be ascending original index), and substring matches ("locker" vs "lock"). Stable-sorting the features array directly also works and removes explicit indices. Follow-ups: features arriving as a stream (same map updates online), or needing top-k popular features (partial sort or heap).
